enonce_markdown: In a rural district of the North West Region the crude birth rate is 38 per 1,000 and the crude death rate is 12 per 1,000. Ignoring migration, what is the annual rate of natural increase of the population?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Natural increase = birth rate minus death rate. Rates per 1,000 are converted to a percentage by dividing by 10.

### Solution

Natural increase = 38 - 12 = 26 per 1,000. As a percentage: 26 / 10 = 2.6% a year.

The wrong options come from adding the two rates (50 per 1,000, i.e. 5.0%), forgetting to convert per 1,000 to a percentage (26%) or dividing by 100 instead of 10 (0.26%).

enonce_markdown: Which statement best summarises the view of Ester Boserup on the relationship between population growth and food supply?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Malthus saw food supply as a limit that population growth overtakes; Boserup reversed the argument and saw population pressure as the stimulus for agricultural change.

### Solution

Boserup argued that rising population density forces farmers to intensify production (shorter fallow, new tools, irrigation, more labour per hectare), so population pressure drives innovation and higher food output.

The statement that population grows geometrically and food arithmetically is Malthus's. The idea that growth is stopped only by war and disease whatever the technology ignores Boserup's point about adaptation, and a fixed food supply that never changes contradicts her argument.

choix.texte: Population grows geometrically while food production grows only arithmetically, so food shortage is inevitable.
Food supply is fixed by nature and population can only be reduced by war and disease.
Population pressure stimulates farmers to intensify production and adopt new techniques, so food output can rise with population.
Population growth has no relationship with agricultural methods because farmers never change their practices.

enonce_markdown: The population of a city is growing at 2.5% a year. Using the rule of 70 (doubling time in years = 70 divided by the annual growth rate in per cent), how long will the population take to double if the rate stays constant?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The rule of 70 gives an approximate doubling time: divide 70 by the growth rate expressed in per cent.

### Solution

Doubling time = 70 / 2.5 = 28 years.

The other options come from dividing by the wrong number (70 / 2 = 35), multiplying instead of dividing (70 x 2.5 = 175) or using 140 as the numerator (140 / 2.5 = 56).

enonce_markdown: A government wants to lower fertility in a poor rural region where many girls leave school early and marry before 16. Which measure is most likely to reduce the birth rate in the long term?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Fertility falls when women are educated, marry later, have work opportunities and are confident that their children will survive.

### Solution

Keeping girls in school and raising the age of marriage delays the start of childbearing and increases women's access to work and information, which lowers family size. It is the measure recommended in the demographic literature.

A tax allowance for each extra child encourages births (a pro-natalist measure). Closing rural clinics would raise infant mortality, and parents who fear losing children tend to have more. A food subsidy for large families also rewards large families.

choix.texte: Giving a tax allowance for each additional child
Keeping girls in school longer and enforcing a higher minimum age of marriage
Closing rural health centres to save money
Subsidising food only for families with more than five children

enonce_markdown: A developing country has a crude birth rate of 40 per 1,000 and a crude death rate of 10 per 1,000, and a population of 20 million. (a) Calculate the natural increase in one year, in persons and in per cent. (b) Explain, with reference to the demographic transition model, why the population is growing so quickly.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Natural increase = births - deaths. In stage 2 of the demographic transition the death rate falls first while the birth rate stays high.

### Solution

(a) Natural increase rate = 40 - 10 = 30 per 1,000 = 3.0% a year. For 20 million people: 20,000,000 x 30 / 1,000 = 600,000 persons in one year.

(b) The country is in stage 2 (early expanding). Death rates have fallen because of better medicine, vaccination, clean water and food supply, but birth rates remain high because of cultural attitudes, the need for farm labour, lack of family planning, early marriage and high infant mortality in the past. The large gap between births and deaths gives rapid growth, and the young age structure means many future parents, so growth continues even if fertility starts to fall (population momentum).

enonce_markdown: Between 2005 and 2015 the population of country X rose from 70 million to 90 million, while the average income per person fell from 600,000 FCFA to 500,000 FCFA a year. (a) Calculate the percentage change in total national income and in income per person. (b) Evaluate whether these figures prove that country X is overpopulated.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Overpopulation means too many people for the resources and technology available, so that living standards are lower than they could be. A fall in income per head while total income rises must be interpreted with care.

### Solution

(a) Total income in 2005 = 70,000,000 x 600,000 = 42,000,000 million FCFA (42 x 10^12). Total income in 2015 = 90,000,000 x 500,000 = 45,000,000 million FCFA (45 x 10^12). Change = (45 - 42) / 42 = +7.1%. Income per person: (500,000 - 600,000) / 600,000 = -16.7%.

(b) The economy grew by 7.1% but the population grew by 28.6% ((90 - 70) / 70), so growth was absorbed by the extra people and each person became poorer. This is consistent with overpopulation, but it does not prove it: a fall in income per head over ten years can also come from falling commodity prices, conflict, poor governance or a young population with a high dependency ratio that has not yet entered the labour force. An evaluation needs further evidence: food supply per person, unemployment, pressure on land and services, and whether better technology or trade could raise output. A balanced conclusion is that the data point towards population pressure on resources but are insufficient on their own.
